provenance.notes: Clean family batch, book archetype, licensed trade. Cheap sweep and inspection in front, real repair tickets behind, sharp autumn spike. Credentials stay as bracketed placeholders; no product or certification-body names. Fresh Fern fails CTA contrast. Ranges are planning figures, not quotes.

pageStructurePlus.contains: What a level one yearly inspection covers, when a level two camera inspection is needed (home sale, new appliance, after a chimney fire), and how each one is booked and reported
pageStructurePlus.why: Buyers hear 'inspection' and don't know which one they need. Explaining the levels stops the phone tag and books the right visit first.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Cracked crowns, leaking flashing, spalling brick, tuckpointing, rebuilds above the roofline and waterproofing, with before-and-after pairs by repair type
pageStructurePlus.why: The repair ticket is where a sweep makes real money, and owners only approve masonry work when they can see it done on a house like theirs.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Stainless liner relining, wood and gas inserts, stove hookups, flue sizing, permits where the town requires them, and what a liner job involves on the day
pageStructurePlus.why: Liner and insert jobs are researched for weeks. A page that explains the job earns the estimate request when they're ready.

pageStructurePlus.section: Caps, dampers and animals in the flue
pageStructurePlus.contains: Chimney caps and spark screens, top-sealing dampers, birds and raccoons in the flue, nesting-season rules, and how removal and capping are priced
pageStructurePlus.why: Scratching in the chimney is an urgent, specific search. A page that names the animal and the fix catches it first.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Smoke spilling into the room, a campfire smell in summer, water stains beside the fireplace, white staining on the brick, and which visit each symptom calls for
pageStructurePlus.why: People search the symptom, not the service. Matching symptom to visit turns a worried search into a booked inspection.

openers.line: Your Google listing has solid chimney sweep reviews and no Website button, so someone planning their first fire of the year can't see what an inspection costs or when you're free.
openers.hook: Open their Maps listing and confirm there is no Website button. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: Where that chimney search could land: {demo-link}

openers.line: The website link on your listing opens Facebook, where your crown and flashing repairs are mixed in with sweep specials from two autumns ago.
openers.hook: Tap their Website link. Note where it lands and the date of the newest repair post.
openers.linkLine: Your chimney repairs and sweep prices on one page: {demo-link}

openers.line: The site on your listing is a free page with a booking form that bounces. In October that form is the difference between a full chimney calendar and a voicemail pile.
openers.hook: Open the site and find one broken thing: a dead form, an old price, a builder banner. Note it.
openers.linkLine: A chimney site with booking that works in October: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your chimney site cut off halfway down on my phone, right where the inspection prices should be. People look this up from the couch in front of a cold fireplace.
openers.hook: Only if they have a site. Load it on your phone and note what breaks. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: Chimney inspections, readable on a phone: {demo-link}

openers.line: There's no price for a sweep or a level one chimney inspection anywhere online. That's the cheap first visit that leads to your repair work, and people book whoever shows a number.
openers.hook: Check the listing, posts and any site for a sweep or inspection price. If there is none, the angle holds.

openers.line: Your crown rebuild and tuckpointing posts are the best chimney repair proof around, and they're buried under sweep reminders on Facebook.
openers.hook: Find one masonry or crown repair post and name the repair if they reply.
openers.linkLine: A chimney repair gallery sorted by job type: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your reviews thank you for finally stopping a leak by the fireplace. That's what a homeowner with a water stain is searching for, and it should sit right next to your chimney repair request.
openers.hook: Read their reviews and copy one phrase about a leak, a smell or a repair. Quote it back if they reply.
openers.linkLine: Your chimney reviews next to the repair request: {demo-link}

openers.line: The first cold weekend, the whole street seems to want a chimney sweep at once. The sweep with open slots online fills October while everyone else returns voicemails.
openers.hook: Use from late August to October. Check for a post about the autumn waitlist or being booked out.

openers.line: Spring and summer are when chimney masonry gets done, but people only think about it when they light a fire. A page that books repair estimates early fills your warm months.
openers.hook: Use from March to June. Look for any masonry or rebuild work in their posts.
openers.linkLine: Chimney repair estimates booked in the warm months: {demo-link}

openers.line: Saw you're hiring a chimney sweep or a mason's helper. Good applicants check whether the company looks steady before they climb a roof for you.
openers.hook: Only if they posted a hiring note or a sign. Note the date.
openers.linkLine: A chimney company page with a hiring section: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your chimney reviews come from {Neighborhood} and other older streets nearby, but nothing online says which towns your truck covers or that you work on old brick.
openers.hook: Find the oldest neighbourhood named in their reviews or posts and use it.
openers.linkLine: Chimney service pages for the towns you cover: {demo-link}

openers.line: A chimney rebuild or a new liner is a big surprise bill. If you offer payment plans, saying so on the repair page keeps people from putting the job off another winter.
openers.hook: Only if they mention financing or payment plans anywhere. Never name a lender.
openers.linkLine: Chimney repairs with payment options explained: {demo-link}

openers.line: Climbing someone's roof and opening their flue is a trust decision. If you're licensed and insured, that belongs in writing on the chimney page beside the Book button.
openers.hook: Look for a licence number, certification or 'insured' on their listing or truck. Use only what they publish, in [brackets] on the demo.
openers.linkLine: Licence and insurance on one chimney page: {demo-link}

openers.line: Sounds like your chimney work runs on the same customers every autumn. That holds until the house sells and the new owner searches for a sweep instead.
openers.hook: Look for reviews that say 'every year' or 'have used them for years'. Quote one.
openers.linkLine: Where a new owner looking for a chimney sweep should land: {demo-link}

openers.line: That {specific recent job} you posted is real chimney work most homeowners never see. It belongs on a page where the next person can request the same repair.
openers.hook: Pick their newest chimney post and name it: the crown, the cap, the liner, the animal.
openers.linkLine: That chimney job on a page that books: {demo-link}

sequence.dm1:
Hi {Owner} — that {specific recent job} you posted is serious chimney work.

I looked for a site for {Business Name} and found the Facebook page, but no way to book a sweep or request a repair estimate before the autumn rush. I put together a sample site with both, with marked placeholders where your photos would go.

Would it help if I sent it over?
sequence.dm2:
{Owner} — following up in case my last message got buried. Here's the sample chimney site for {Business Name}: {demo-link}

It has sweep and inspection booking, the inspection levels explained, a masonry repair gallery and a repair request with photo upload. If it's not useful, tell me and I'll leave you alone.
sequence.call:
"Hi, is this {Owner}? I'm {Your Name}, I build websites for chimney companies here in {City}. I sent you a message a couple of days ago, did it come through?"

IF NO:
"No surprise, it's your busy season. Short version: I built a sample site for {Business Name} that books sweeps and inspections online and takes repair requests with photos, with marked placeholders where your photos would go. Can I text you the link?"

IF YES:
"What did you think?"
 → let them talk, don't fill the silence
"The build runs {Build Range}, then {Care Range} a month for hosting and changes. For a chimney company your size I'd normally quote about {Build Price}. One crown repair covers it."
"Can I walk you through it for ten minutes, maybe after you're off the roof one evening?"

CLOSE:
"I'll send a one-page scope and a deposit invoice. We start the day it clears."

objections.handler: "Then the site does the booking for next year and fills your spring and summer with masonry estimates, which is the work you want in the warm months anyway."

objections.objection: All my work is repeat customers.
objections.handler: "That's a good chimney business. Houses sell, though, and every new owner searches for a sweep. The site is what they find instead of the franchise ad."

objections.objection: Sweeps are cheap, I don't need a fancy site.
objections.handler: "The sweep is cheap. The crown, the liner and the rebuild aren't. The site sells the inspection, and the inspection sells the repair."

objections.objection: I don't want to put repair prices online.
objections.handler: "You don't have to. Post the sweep and inspection price, and let repairs come in as a request with photos. You quote those after you look."

objections.objection: I'm on one of those lead apps.
objections.handler: "Those leads go to several chimney companies at once and you pay either way. Someone who finds your own site only gets you."
"{Build Range}. For you about {Build Price}, because it's booking, the inspection levels page, the repair request and the masonry gallery. One crown or flashing repair pays for it."

email.subject: Chimney site for {Business Name}

sequence.voicemail: "Hi {Owner}, it's {Your Name}. I build websites for chimney companies in {City}, and I made a sample site for {Business Name} that books sweeps and takes repair requests online. I'll text you the link. {Your Phone}. Thanks."
sequence.takedown:
{Owner} — I'm taking the {Business Name} chimney demo down on Friday to free up the space.

Want me to leave it up? One word is fine either way.
sequence.nurture:
Hi {Owner} — the autumn chimney rush in {City} is close to its peak, and the next window is spring masonry season. Thought of you.

The site is still here whenever you want it, and nothing's changed on price. {demo-link} if you want another look.

bullets: Peg the build to one crown or flashing repair, never to the price of a sweep.
Sweep and inspection booking is the core. Price the repair request, gallery and liner page around it.
Price the repair request higher when it takes photos and routes to a site-visit calendar; that is the money path.
Charge per page for liners, caps and animals, and real estate inspections; each one is a separate search.
Never write a credential into the copy the prospect hasn't published. Leave a bracketed slot and charge nothing extra to fill it.
Keep monthly items small next to one sweep, so the owner doesn't weigh them against a visit.

lineItems.item: Repair request with photo upload and site-visit booking
lineItems.description: Max when it asks repair type, roof pitch and access, takes several photos and offers estimate slots from the owner's calendar.
Max with before-and-after pairs sorted by crowns, flashing, tuckpointing and rebuilds, with a short caption per job.
Max with a fuel-type question set, what a reline involves on the day, permit notes and an estimate request.
Max with a closing-date field, agent contact fields and a sample report layout for buyers and sellers.
Max with an urgent request form, cap options and the owner's nesting-season policy written out.

lineItems.item: Payment options explainer for big repairs
lineItems.description: Max when it explains deposits, staged payments and any plan they already offer, without naming a lender.
Max when each page names the housing age and common chimney types there, with repairs done in that town.

withoutAI.route: Roofers who work around the chimney
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The roofer who calls you about flashing before a re-roof has an old gallery and no estimate form. Introduce me."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Roofers have bigger tickets and budgets, and they trust the chimney company that makes their flashing work.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The stove shop that sends you liner installs has a showroom nobody can browse online. Your chimney work gets me in the door."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Hearth shops sell the insert and need the installer; they already rely on the sweep.

withoutAI.route: Home inspectors who refer chimney work
withoutAI.whoPays: The inspector, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The inspector who refers buyers to you for a chimney camera scan books by phone. A booking site with sample reports fixes that."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Inspectors are small shops that need sites, and they trust the sweep they send work to.

withoutAI.whoPays: The firewood seller, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The firewood guy who delivers to your chimney customers takes orders by text. An order page with delivery days is a small build."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Same customers, same season, and the firewood seller is happy to pass the sweep's name along.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The mason you hand the big chimney rebuilds to shows his work on Facebook only. A portfolio page with an estimate request is my next build."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Masons get sizable jobs and listen when the sweep who feeds them work recommends you.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The historic district group whose members call you for old chimney work needs a site with approved-contractor lists and guidelines."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Associations pay for member resources and trust the chimney company already working on their houses.

withAI.pitchLine: "Homeowners upload a photo of a ceiling stain, and the triage sorts likely roof leaks from chimney flashing leaks before anyone climbs."
withAI.whyItWorks: Roofers waste trips on chimney leaks. The sweep who gets those referrals benefits too.

withAI.route: Stove and insert matcher for the hearth shop
withAI.pitchLine: "Shoppers describe the room, the fireplace and the fuel, and the matcher suggests inserts the shop stocks and books the chimney liner check."
withAI.whyItWorks: Shops lose browsers who can't decide. The sweep's liner work follows every sale.

withAI.pitchLine: "Inspectors talk through each house, and the draft report flags chimney and fireplace items for a specialist, ready to edit."
withAI.whyItWorks: Inspectors write reports nightly, and every chimney flag is a referral for the client.

withAI.route: Delivery scheduler for the firewood seller
withAI.pitchLine: "Customers text how much firewood they want, and the scheduler groups deliveries by street and reminds them to book the chimney sweep first."
withAI.whyItWorks: Small sellers run on text messages and love anything that saves a weekend. The sweep gets a nudge on every order.

withAI.pitchLine: "The mason talks through a chimney rebuild on site and gets a draft estimate with materials and stages, ready to send."
withAI.whyItWorks: Masons hate paperwork, and the sweep who refers them sees how slow their quotes are.

withAI.whoPays: The association or district office, monthly
withAI.pitchLine: "Owners ask whether they can change a chimney cap or rebuild with new brick, and the assistant answers from the district's own guidelines."
withAI.whyItWorks: District staff answer the same questions all year, and the chimney company is the trusted contractor in the room.

softwareAI.name: Missed-call text-back with sweep slots
softwareAI.pitchLine: "You're on a roof in October and can't answer. The caller gets a text with the chimney sweep price and the next open days within a minute."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Day 30. Needs the business number forwarded and wording they approve.

softwareAI.name: Yearly sweep reminder before burn season
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every August, last year's chimney customers get a text with their address filled in and early sweep slots before the rush."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs a list of past jobs with dates.

softwareAI.name: Inspection report builder with photos
softwareAI.pitchLine: "The sweep ticks the checklist, adds roof and flue photos, and the homeowner gets a clean chimney inspection report before the truck leaves."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs their inspection checklist and report wording.

softwareAI.name: Booking chat for chimney questions
softwareAI.pitchLine: "It answers 'which inspection do I need to sell my house' and 'do you remove birds' from your own chimney answers, then books the visit."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs services, prices, inspection rules and the calendar. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Review reply drafts for chimney jobs
softwareAI.pitchLine: "A customer thanks you for fixing the smoky fireplace; a warm reply mentioning that chimney job is drafted and waiting when you climb down."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2, alongside review requests. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Repair estimate builder
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Pick crown, flashing, cap or tuckpointing, enter the measurements, and the chimney repair estimate goes out with photos while you're still in the driveway."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs their repair pricing rules and material costs.

softwareAI.name: Repair photo reader for estimate requests
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Homeowners upload photos of a cracked crown or a water stain, and you get a draft note on the likely chimney repair and which visit to book."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs past repair photos with what the job turned out to be. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Autumn waitlist and cancellation filler
softwareAI.pitchLine: "When October is full, people join a chimney sweep waitlist by town, and a cancellation goes to the nearest one first."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3, before the autumn rush. Needs the calendar and their service towns.

softwareAI.name: After-hours receptionist for smoke and animal calls
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Someone calls at night about smoke in the room or scratching in the chimney, hears the owner's approved wording, and gets the first slot."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs the calendar, prices and the owner's approved urgent-call wording. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Job photo log by address
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every chimney you've touched, with flue photos and notes by year, so next autumn's inspection starts from last year's findings."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs past job records and photos, even from a phone.

softwareAI.name: Sweep and mason applicant screener
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Applicants for chimney sweep and mason's helper jobs answer questions about heights, driving and early starts, and you only call the good fits."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Any month they're hiring. Needs must-haves, pay and schedule. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Repair follow-up from inspection findings
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every inspection that found a chimney problem gets a follow-up a few weeks later with the photos and the repair estimate, before the owner forgets."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3, after the report builder. Needs the report data and approved wording.

softwareAI.name: Route planner by town and roof type
softwareAI.pitchLine: "October chimney sweeps grouped by town, with steep roofs flagged for the two-person crew, so each day is planned before dawn."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs job addresses, crews and roof notes.

softwareAI.name: Customer message sorter for chimney jobs
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Reschedules, 'can I use the fireplace tonight' questions and estimate follow-ups get sorted and drafted for the owner's approval."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs the business text line or inbox. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Job costing per chimney repair
softwareAI.pitchLine: "See what each crown, liner and rebuild actually made once mortar, metal and labour are counted, so the next chimney estimate is priced right."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs a few months of repair tickets and material costs.

softwareAI.name: Masonry season scheduler
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Approved chimney repairs from the autumn get slotted into spring and summer by weather window, with customers told their week ahead."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs the list of approved repairs and crew capacity.

softwareAI.name: Real estate inspection report template
softwareAI.pitchLine: "A chimney report layout a buyer's agent can read in a minute, with findings, photos and repairs listed, sent to both agents on closing deadlines."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5, after the report builder. Needs a few past real estate reports.

softwareAI.name: Crew knowledge base for flue and liner jobs
softwareAI.pitchLine: "A new sweep asks the phone how the owner wants a liner sized or a cap measured, and gets the owner's own answer on the roof."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs written procedures and the owner's approval of every answer. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Estimate follow-up writer
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Unsigned chimney repair estimates get a short, polite follow-up in your voice that answers the question the owner probably had."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4, after the estimate builder. Needs past estimates and outcomes. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Deposit request on approved repairs
softwareAI.pitchLine: "When a homeowner approves a chimney repair estimate, the deposit request and the scheduling link go out the same minute."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs their deposit rules and payment method.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Productise the chimney inspection report builder
routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: Chimney sweep companies, monthly per account
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "I built a chimney inspection report tool for one sweep. Every sweep in the country writes the same report on a clipboard."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: The first client paid for the workflow, and the report is the same task for every sweep doing inspections.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: License the repair estimate builder to a chimney supply distributor
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Give every sweep who buys caps and liners from you an estimate builder that prices with your catalog."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Distributors want sweeps ordering from them, and an estimate tool that uses their parts list does it.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Chimney sweep guild or association toolkit
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Offer every member sweep a site template with the inspection levels page and a repair request built in."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Associations want members looking professional, and one agreement reaches many owners.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your installer list is a spreadsheet. A locator that sends buyers to vetted chimney and liner installers sells more inserts."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Manufacturers need installers to move product, and the chimney client proves you know the install side.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: White-label chimney site template for agencies
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your agency keeps getting chimney sweeps as clients. License my template with booking, inspection levels and the masonry gallery done."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Agencies sell the client; you sell them the part you've already got right.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Home inspection franchises' specialist referral page
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "When your inspectors flag a chimney, the buyer gets one page of vetted local sweeps with camera inspection slots."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Inspection firms want to refer without liability, and a vetted specialist page lets them.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The city or county preservation office
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Owners of old houses need chimney and masonry guidance that matches district rules. One page with guidelines and approved trades."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Preservation offices have small budgets for public resources, and the chimney client is credible on old masonry.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: A regional insurer or agency, annually
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Policyholders with wood-burning fireplaces get a yearly reminder and a booking page with vetted local sweeps."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Insurers like maintenance programs, and the sweep client already sends the reminders and reports.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: The same chimney stack in the next metro
routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: New chimney clients in a new metro
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "I build for one sweep per area, and {City} is spoken for. The older towns up the highway are wide open."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Non-competing geography lets you reuse the inspection levels page, the gallery layout and the proof.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Firewood and hearth retailers' care program
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Every cord of firewood or stove you sell comes with a card that books a chimney sweep before the first fire."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Retailers want the customer happy and safe-feeling, and the sweep earns the visit.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Every rental with a fireplace gets its yearly chimney sweep scheduled and the report filed, across your whole portfolio."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Managers need records and dread tenant fireplace calls; the sweep client already does the work.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "If a developer left your sweep scheduler half-built, October is a bad month to find out. I finish chimney tools that others walked away from."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Stranded owners already decided to buy; they want someone who has finished one.
